power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background information (e.g., age, gender, and field of study) was obtained from the university student register in accordance with applicable research permissions and data protection regulations.

Student agency has gained increasing attention in higher education (HE) research, driven by its recognized importance for learning, well-being, and students' capacity to engage meaningfully with complex societal challenges (Inouye et al., 2023; Lund & Vestøl, 2020; Marín et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Student agency has gained increasing attention in higher education (HE) research, driven by its recognized importance for learning, well-being, and students' capacity to engage meaningfully with complex societal challenges <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Inouye et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Lund & Vestøl, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Marín et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Yang et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond academic performance, agency has been linked to students' personal growth, sense of connectedness, and preparedness for transitions from education to work life (Ross et al., 2024; Schoon & Heckhausen, 2019).
text.formatted: Beyond academic performance, agency has been linked to students' personal growth, sense of connectedness, and preparedness for transitions from education to work life <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Ross et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Schoon & Heckhausen, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, educational policy documents emphasize student agency as a central goal of education (OECD, n.d.).
Yet agency is not only an educational outcome.
It is enacted within everyday learning situations, making it important to understand how course-level pedagogical conditions relate to students' agency.

Nevertheless, understanding of agency remains conceptually and empirically fragmented: Prior reviews have highlighted persistent challenges, including undertheorization, reliance on narrow or unidimensional representations of agency, and limited integration between theoretical models and empirical measurement (Marín et al., 2020; Stenalt & Lassesen, 2021).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, understanding of agency remains conceptually and empirically fragmented: Prior reviews have highlighted persistent challenges, including undertheorization, reliance on narrow or unidimensional representations of agency, and limited integration between theoretical models and empirical measurement <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Marín et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Stenalt & Lassesen, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Empirical research has often focused on specific groups of students or isolated pedagogical interventions, leaving open questions about how agency is experienced across different pedagogical settings and how it relates systematically to teaching practices.

There is limited understanding of how student agency is constituted in course-level micro-contexts that organize students' work and participation and how it can be meaningfully supported through pedagogy.

This study addresses these gaps by examining university students' perceptions of their agency within a multidimensional framework comprising three analytically distinct components: resources for agency, agentic will, and agentic action.

The study contributes to understanding how these perceptions vary across students and course contexts, how the three components of agency relate to one another, and how they are associated with the teaching practices students encounter in courses within their fields of study.

A studentinformed perspective is particularly important because students are uniquely positioned to evaluate both their perceived opportunities for agency and their own volitional orientations and actions in educational contexts.

To address these aims, we pose the following research questions (RQ): RQ1: How do university students perceive their agency across the three components of agency: resources for agency, agentic will, and agentic action (i.e., are there differences in the levels of students' perceptions across the subdimensions)?
To what extent is variation in these perceptions attributable to student-and courselevel differences?
RQ3: How are the three components of agency and their subdimensions interrelated?

How are students' perceptions of agency associated with their ratings of teaching practices with respect to course design transparency, different types of learning activities, and student-teacher roles in their courses?
Our conceptualization draws on core qualities of agency highlighted in the literaturesnamely, views of agency as subjectively experienced, socially embedded, and dynamically evolving.

First, we understand agency as extending beyond observable action or participation and as rooted in students' experiences of ownership, influence, and possibilities for learning (e.g., Case, 2015; Cook-Sather, 2020; Su, 2011).

text.text: Second, we view agency as being formed in interaction with social, relational, and structural conditions rather than evolving solely as an individual attribute (e.g., Archer, 2003; Matusov et al., 2016).

text.text: Third, we see that agency unfolds in the dynamic interplay between learners and their environments, with the potential for both adaptation and transformation (Lund & Vestøl, 2020; Mezirow, 2000).

text.text: Based on these qualities, we conceptualize student agency as a dynamically evolving and contextually shaped capacity for purposeful learning and transformation, which is enabled by students' self-perceived resources for agency, manifested in their agentic will and realized through their agentic action.

Operationally, we approach this capacity as comprising three interrelated components: (1) students' self-perceived resources for agency (e.g., experiences of interactional support, personal capabilities, and environmental affordances for influence), (2) their self-reported agentic will (e.g., willingness to set demanding goals, invest effort in interactive learning, and seize opportunities to engage in joint problem-solving and to influence learning practices), and (3) their self-reported agentic action through which they intentionally advance their learning, contribute to knowledge co-construction with other learners, and influence learning processes and conditions in their courses.
While conceptually distinct, these components and their respective subdimensions are assumed to be dynamically interconnected in the enactment of student agency.

Together, they form the Agency of University Students -Resources, Will, and Action (AUS-RWA) model (Fig. 1), developed as part of our ongoing research on student agency (Jääskelä, et al., 2017 (Jääskelä, et al., , 2020 (Jääskelä, et al., , 2023)).

text.text: By examining the subdimensions of agency and their associations with teaching practices while taking into account the clustering of students within courses, the study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of how agency is shaped and supported in HE.

text.text: On the other hand, sociocultural and sociological perspectives emphasize that agency is shaped in relation to interaction with social and structural conditions.

A further defining quality of student agency is its dynamic nature, which includes the potential for transformation.
Agency develops through learners' ongoing participation, interaction, and reflection in educational settings.

text.text: We argue that the core qualities of subjectivity, social and structural embeddedness, and dynamic development of agency connect individuals' experiences with the structural conditions of learning environments.
This implies that agency is likely to vary across educational contexts, highlighting the importance of examining both individual-and course-level variation.

Our multidimensional conceptualization of student agency distinguishes between three interrelated components: students' perceived resources for agency, their agentic will, and the action through which agency is enacted.

text.text: In the AUS-RWA model, agentic will represents the relationally and motivationally mediated volitional impulse-that is, an intentional willingness and orientation toward engagement in agentic action within specific learning situations.

text.text: Whereas Klemenčič conceptualized the will to act broadly as a general agentic orientation toward action, our conceptualization of agentic will focuses more specifically on students' readiness and commitment to mobilize available capabilities, opportunities, and situational resources toward purposeful learning-related action.

This conceptualization builds on a relational understanding of agency, which views agency as emerging from the dynamic interplay between individuals and their social, cultural, and material environments (Biesta & Tedder, 2007; Emirbayer & Mische, 1998).

text.text: Accordingly, in the AUS-RWA model, we see that students' agentic will develops in relation to their perceptions of personal capabilities, relational resources, and opportunities for agency.
The perceived resources provide a basis for agentic will but do not fully determine it.
Thus, motivationally, agentic will concerns the value students attribute to engaging agentically in learning and striving to take up and tackle challenges.
Volitionally, will concerns students' willingness to invest effort and sustain commitment despite challenges or competing demands.

Given that agency is shaped by the interplay between individuals and social and structural conditions (Archer, 2003), and that within HE, these conditions are typically manifested in course-level pedagogical arrangements and organized forms of participation (Damşa et al., 2010; Eteläpelto & Lahti, 2008), teaching practices constitute an important focus of the present analysis.

text.text: Rather than viewing teaching practices as mere resources for agency, we conceptualize them as pedagogical arrangements that structure the opportunities and conditions through which student agency emerges and can be enacted.

Although previous research has not always examined teaching practices explicitly through the lens of agency, several pedagogical features appear relevant for supporting students' participation, influence, and active involvement in learning (e.g., Goodyear & Dudley, 2015; Moses et al., 2020; Nieminen et al., 2022a; Sjølie et al., 2022).

text.text: The present study focuses on three such features: transparency of course design, active learning activities, and student-teacher roles.

Aspects of transparent course design, such as clear articulation of learning objectives, alignment between goals and assessment, and explicit communication of expectations, have been linked to increased student engagement and understanding (Anderson et al., 2013; Levinsson et al., 2024; Winkelmes et al., 2016).

text.text: Although agency has not been typically examined as an outcome in this line of research, transparent course design may create conditions that enable students to take a more active role in their learning by making purposeful choices about their goals and study strategies and strengthening their sense of control over learning.
Learning activities that involve authentic problem-solving, collaboration, and reflection may also support student agency.

Collaborative problem-solving, inquiry-based tasks, and project-based learning provide opportunities for students to take responsibility and engage in meaningful knowledge construction (Jiang et al., 2022; Nieminen et al., 2022a; Sjølie et al., 2022).

text.text: Similarly, practices such as self-assessment and co-creation can support students' evaluative judgment, self-regulation, and sense of ownership (Boud & Molloy, 2013; Bovill et al., 2016; Nieminen & Tuohilampi, 2020).

text.text: Student-teacher roles can also shape how opportunities for agency are created and distributed within learning environments.

A shift toward facilitative and partnershiporiented teacher roles has been linked to greater opportunities for student participation, expressing one's own voice, and having an impact in learning processes, thereby creating conditions that support the enactment of agency (Goodyear & Dudley, 2015; Moses et al., 2020; Robertson, 2017).

text.text: Although these strands of research highlight several pedagogical features that may support student agency, empirical work examining their relationships with multidimensional conceptualizations of agency across course contexts remains limited.
This study addresses this gap by analyzing how students' perceptions of teaching practices relate to students' perceived resources for agency, agentic will, and agentic action.
>Methods
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Methods</head>

text.text: This study involved 1,140 students enrolled in 47 undergraduate courses (primarily bachelor's degree programs) at a Finnish research university.
Of these, 337 (29.6%) were male, 801 (70.3%) were female, and two did not disclose their gender.
The participants' ages ranged from 18 to 66 years (M = 24.59, SD = 6.89).
The courses represented the academic fields in natural sciences, information technology, business and economics, educational sciences, humanities, and sport and health sciences.
On average, 24.3 students participated in each course (range = 10-72, SD = 15.8).
The students were informed of the study aims and the voluntary nature of participation, and written consent was obtained from all participants.
Data were collected via an online questionnaire administered at the latter part of each course between spring 2023 and spring 2024.

The questionnaire included items measuring students' perceptions of their agency, as well as items asking about their perceptions of teaching practices in the course they were attending at the time of completion.
Demographic information was retrieved from the university's student register.

Teaching practices were measured using student ratings of three dimensions: (1) learning activities, (2) course design transparency, and (3) student-teacher roles in their course.
Learning activities (LA) were assessed by asking students to rate the extent to which different types of learning activities were included in their course.
They responded to 15 items on a five-point Likert scale, with1 = not at all,2 = little or rarely,3 = moderately,4 = a lot or often, and5 = very much or continuously.

The items were developed based on previous studies that found positive links between single aspects of student agency (e.g., self-efficacy beliefs, agentic goal-oriented action, influential participation) and active learning practices (e.g., content knowledge-focused, collaborative, (self)regulative, feedback activities) (e.g., Jiang et al., 2022; Lipponen & Kumpulainen, 2011; Moses et al., 2020; Nieminen & Tuohilampi, 2020; Sjølie et al., 2022).

text.text: In the confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) three factors were identified (Appendix B): (1) Tasks demanding higherorder thinking (four items; e.g., problem-solving tasks, critical evaluation of knowledge); (2) Interactive student collaboration (four items; e.g., small-group work around learning tasks, sharing reasoning or reflections, feedback on other's work); and (3) Monitoring and support for personal learning (seven items; e.g., self-assessment of learning, teacher identification of student challenges, and teacher guidance of individual students).

Course design transparency (CDT) was examined by asking the students to rate the extent to which five course design elements were made explicit and negotiated with them in their course: (1) learning objectives, (2) working methods, (3) timetable, (4) evaluation criteria, and (5) assessment methods.

Transparency in these elements has been shown to promote student agency by helping students orient to their studies, make informed decisions, and engage in their work (e.g., Anderson et al., 2013; King et al., 2024).

Student-teacher roles (STR) were measured using one multiple-choice item with four response options in which the students selected the description that best reflected the distribution of responsibilities between the teacher and themselves in their course.
The abbreviated multiple-choice options were as follows: (1) The teacher manages and assesses the achievement of learning outcomes.

Students' role is to complete the given tasks. ( 2)The teacher has the role of the supervisor of learning by determining course implementation and assessment but adapting to students different learning needs and making modifications.

WLSMV was selected because the items were ordinal and, in some cases, responses were skewed, with answers limited to three of the five categories.
The sample size (n = 1,140) was sufficient for this procedure, with a minimum group size of 10 individuals (Park, 2023).

Missing values were assumed to be missing at random.
As the data had a nested structure (individual students situated in groups), multilevel analyses were considered appropriate.
To address the second research question, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) were calculated to examine the extent to which variation was attributable to student-and course-level differences.

text.text: To address the fourth research question, we examined associations between agency and teaching practices using multilevel SEM.
In the first regression model, the latent CDT factor was specified as an independent variable, with the latent student agency factors as dependent variables.
In the second regression model, the three latent LA factors were specified as independent variables, with the latent student agency factors as dependent variables.

Because the LA factors (F1-F3) were highly correlated (Appendix B), multicollinearity was addressed using Cholesky decomposition, which enables hierarchical regression within the SEM framework and yields more interpretable results (de Jong, 1999).
Wald tests were conducted to compare mean differences in the latent student agency factors across STR categories.
All analyses controlled for between-course variation using multilevel modeling.
Model fit was evaluated using the comparative fit index (CFI), Tucker-Lewis index (TLI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), and standardized root mean square residual (SRMR).
The following thresholds were applied to indicate a good model fit: CFI and TLI > .95, RMSEA < .06, and SRMR < .08 (Hu & Bentler, 1999).

The results showed that the means of the students' perceptions of their agency were statistically significantly lower on most factors when they viewed their instructor's role as a manager who managed the course and its progression and assessed the achievement of learning outcomes, compared to when they perceived their instructor as a supervisor who considered their learning needs or when they perceived their instructor as a partner collaborating with students.

Specifically, the instructor's role as a manager was associated with lower levels of opportunities for interactive learning, for being heard and having impact, for renewal of one's thinking, and for trust in teacher support (agency resources).

In contrast, teacher roles that involved considering students' learning needs or partnering with students were linked to somewhat higher levels of these same agency resources, as perceived by students.
Notably, perceiving the instructor as a supervisor who considered students' learning needs was associated with higher ratings of trust in teacher support compared with other role categories.
The R² values indicated that STR explained 9.7% of the variance in opportunities for interactive learning, 8.1% in being heard and having impact, and 5.6% in trust in teacher support.
Taken together, STR accounted for only a small proportion of the variance (under 5%) in most agency factors.

This study examined student agency in higher education (HE) as a multidimensional and multilevel phenomenon comprising students' perceptions of their agency resources, their agentic will, and agentic action.

Moving beyond approaches that focus on observable manifestations or outcomes of agency-such as active participation or agentic engagement-the study conceptualizes agency as a dynamic configuration through which students make interpretations and position themselves within learning environments and thereby develop their multidimensional capacity for purposeful learning.

The findings contribute to research on agency in three ways: First, they provide empirical support for conceptualizing agency as a multidimensional construct with analytically distinct yet interrelated components.

Second, our findings demonstrate the need to take into account the multilevel nature of agency as students' perceptions of their agency were found to vary both within and between courses, indicating that agency is responsive to contextual conditions.

Third, the present study identified systematic associations between teaching practices and different dimensions of agency, suggesting that pedagogical arrangements in the courses play an important role in shaping the conditions under which student agency is enacted.
Overall, students reported moderate to high levels of agency across HE courses.
However, variation across subdimensions revealed some interesting differences or tensions in how agency is experienced and enacted.
The high perceived power balance among students in their courses indicates that learning environments were typically perceived socially safe and relatively non-hierarchical.

Yet, lower ratings for peer support -and notable differences compared to ratings of power balance (d = 0.80) and trust in teacher support (d = 0.66)-suggest that the perceived power balance among students does not automatically translate into experiences of supportive peer resources.

Relational perspectives presented in prior literature emphasize that agency is shaped by the positions individuals are afforded within social practices and by their access to participation (Eteläpelto & Lahti, 2008).
text.formatted: Relational perspectives presented in prior literature emphasize that agency is shaped by the positions individuals are afforded within social practices and by their access to participation <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Eteläpelto & Lahti, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, students' experiences of power balance appear to mostly reflect equal opportunities to participate in study groups, whereas supportive peer resources are more likely to come into view where joint work is orchestrated and facilitated (Damşa et al., 2011; Lipponen & Kumpulainen, 2011), especially when attention is also directed to fostering constructive peer support.
text.formatted: Therefore, students' experiences of power balance appear to mostly reflect equal opportunities to participate in study groups, whereas supportive peer resources are more likely to come into view where joint work is orchestrated and facilitated <ref type="bibr">(Damşa et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Lipponen & Kumpulainen, 2011)</ref>, especially when attention is also directed to fostering constructive peer support.

text.text: A further tension was observed between the students' will to engage and their perceived opportunities for interaction.

Students reported relatively high willingness to engage in interactive learning, but this was only moderately reflected in their ratings of perceived opportunities for interactive learning (d = 0.52), and even less in their ratings of active impactful participation-the lowest-rated subdimension.
Similarly, while students recognized opportunities for renewal of thinking, these did not consistently translate into enacted participatory agency (d = 0.94).
This gap between potential and enactment indicates that agency is not solely an individual disposition but depends on how learning environments structure opportunities for action.

Previous studies have shown that dialogic engagement and the co-construction of knowledge rarely emerge spontaneously. Mercer (2012) demonstrates that such forms of participation develop when teachers establish shared norms and routines for interaction, while Chang and Brickman (2018) highlight that collaborative learning more broadly depends on clear task structures and instructional support.

text.text: Dimensions directly linked to teachers' action-such as students' trust in teacher support and opportunities for being heard and having influence-formed a strong relational foundation for agency.
On average, students perceived that they were listened to, could express their views, and received support from the teacher when facing challenges.
However, the gap between being heard and active participation (d = 0.33) may imply that courses differ in the extent to which they invite participatory or transformative forms of agency.

This interpretation is consistent with previous research, which indicates that participation depends on reciprocal interaction and the gradual construction of shared understanding (Mercer, 2012; Damşa et al., 2011) and may remain limited by insufficient self-efficacy (Bandura, 2006).
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with previous research, which indicates that participation depends on reciprocal interaction and the gradual construction of shared understanding <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Mercer, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Damşa et al., 2011)</ref> and may remain limited by insufficient self-efficacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bandura, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, the findings indicate that agency-supportive conditions are unevenly realized across their dimensions.
While teacher-student relations and supportive structures appear relatively well established, peer support and active participation remain less developed.

This highlights the importance of pedagogical practices that actively foster dialogic engagement and collaborative knowledge construction; without such orchestration, available resources may not fully translate into enacted student agency (Mercer, 2012; Damşa et al., 2011).
text.formatted: This highlights the importance of pedagogical practices that actively foster dialogic engagement and collaborative knowledge construction; without such orchestration, available resources may not fully translate into enacted student agency <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Mercer, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Damşa et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Our multilevel analysis demonstrated that student agency is not solely an individuallevel phenomenon.

While a substantial proportion of variance was attributable to differences between students, the significant between-course variation was also nonnegligible, particularly in students' opportunities for interactive learning; being heard and having impact; their competence beliefs; opportunities for renewal of one's thinking; and their active, impactful participation.

These patterns suggest that students' experiences of their agency partly vary across course contexts, supporting relational perspectives that view agency as emerging through the interplay between learners and the educational environments in which they participate.

This aligns with prior research indicating that learning environments and pedagogical practices shape students' opportunities for participation and influence and thereby condition how agency can be enacted in different contexts (Damşa et al., 2011; Juutilainen, et al., 2018; Klemenčič, 2017; Stenalt & Lassesen, 2021).
text.formatted: This aligns with prior research indicating that learning environments and pedagogical practices shape students' opportunities for participation and influence and thereby condition how agency can be enacted in different contexts <ref type="bibr">(Damşa et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Juutilainen, et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Klemenčič, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Stenalt & Lassesen, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, substantial individual-level variation-especially for self-efficacy beliefs, relational resources, and students' will to engage in and contribute to (co)learning-indicates that agency is also shaped by how students perceive and take up these opportunities.
Consistent with prior literature, this highlights that individual differences remain central to how students interpret and act within given conditions (Bandura, 2018; Mercer, 2012). Mercer, 2012).
text.formatted: Consistent with prior literature, this highlights that individual differences remain central to how students interpret and act within given conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bandura, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Mercer, 2012)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Mercer, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, the findings support a multilevel understanding of agency as both individually experienced and pedagogically structured.

Rather than being a stable individual attribute, agency presents itself as a context-sensitive phenomenon that emerges through the interaction between students' agentic will and their perceived opportunities afforded by features such as course design and pedagogical practices.

Our analyses show that the subdimensions capturing agency resources, students' agentic will, and agentic action are empirically related in ways that are consistent with the proposed multidimensional conceptual model.
Correlational patterns at both the individual and course levels indicate systematic associations across subdimensions, although the strength of these associations varies.
Particularly strong associations were observed between striving for understanding (will) and intentional, goal-directed learning (action).

These findings contribute to the literature by providing a novel multidimensional conceptualization of student agency that brings together agency resources, agentic will, and agentic action into a unified framework.
The results lend support to the conceptualization of agency as a multidimensional construct comprising analytically distinct yet interrelated components.
At the same time, some subdimensions appear to be more closely associated than others.

For example, the strong association between striving for understanding and intentional, goal-directed learning suggests that students' willingness to invest effort in learning and embrace challenges tends to co-occur with purposeful, goaldirected learning and reflective engagement in learning, which represent conceptually distinct subdimensions of agency.
In the AUS-RWA model, resources for agency, agentic will, and agentic action constitute three interconnected components of agency.

The observed correlations among the components support their empirical connections, suggesting that students' perceptions of resources for agency in their course, their agentic will, and their agentic action are interrelated.

In the AUS-RWA framework, resources capture both personal capabilities and contextual opportunities for agency, while agentic will reflects students' willingness to mobilize these resources toward purposeful learning, and agentic action represents the enactment of this will in specific learning situations.
However, the present findings do not allow conclusions about the directionality or underlying mechanisms of these relationships.

Future longitudinal, process-oriented, and comparative research is needed to examine how these dimensions interact and develop over time and whether the patterns observed in this study can be replicated across different educational and cultural contexts.
The associations between teaching practices and student agency suggest that pedagogy shapes conditions under which agency can evolve.
Different practices appear to activate or support different dimensions of agency.

From the teacher orchestrated learning activities organized in the courses, those requiring higher-order thinking, such as problem-solving and critical evaluation of knowledge, were more strongly associated with student agency.

These activities showed consistent links with student-perceived opportunities to renew thinking (resource), as well as with students' agentic will and agentic action, suggesting that cognitively demanding tasks in particular may activate higher education students' willingness to invest effort and engage in intentional action.

This aligns with prior research showing that inquiry-based and problem-based learning foster students' active engagement and responsibility for their own learning (Jiang et al., 2022; Lipponen & Kumpulainen, 2011).
text.formatted: This aligns with prior research showing that inquiry-based and problem-based learning foster students' active engagement and responsibility for their own learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Jiang et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Lipponen & Kumpulainen, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The relatively weak association between higher-order tasks and competence beliefs suggests that cognitively challenging tasks alone do not automatically foster a sense of capability.

This highlights the importance of instructional scaffolding and feedback that help students view demanding tasks as manageable: without sufficient support demanding tasks require effort but do not strengthen perceived competence.

Student perceptions of collaborative learning practices showed a complex pattern where interactive student activities, such as small-group work and joint project work, were positively associated with high perceived resources of peer support (both receiving and offering it).

However, collaborative activities had weaker links to students' willingness to invest effort and engage in collaborative work, and enact intentional, goal-directed learning, and they were negatively associated with trust in teacher support.
This suggests that interactive working methods do not automatically foster agentic engagement.
Rather, collaboration may require task framing and guidance to translate into active participation (Chang & Brickman, 2018; Damşa et al., 2011; Lipponen & Kumpulainen, 2011).
text.formatted: Rather, collaboration may require task framing and guidance to translate into active participation <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Chang & Brickman, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Damşa et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Lipponen & Kumpulainen, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Prior research similarly suggests that collaborative practices can support epistemic agency when appropriately designed (Nieminen et al., 2022a).
text.formatted: Prior research similarly suggests that collaborative practices can support epistemic agency when appropriately designed <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Nieminen et al., 2022a)</ref>.

text.text: Practices focused on monitoring and supporting personal learning had moderate associations with trust in teacher support and perceptions of being heard and having impact (resources) but no significant relationships with other agency factors.
Transparency in course design was positively, albeit modestly, associated with all subdimensions of agency, particularly when course features were negotiated with students.

These findings align with previous research demonstrating that transparency enhances students' understanding and engagement, and sense of control (Anderson et al., 2013; Evans, 2016; Winkelmes et al., 2016).
text.formatted: These findings align with previous research demonstrating that transparency enhances students' understanding and engagement, and sense of control <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Anderson et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Evans, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Winkelmes et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The present results extend this work by indicating that course transparency supports student agency across multiple dimensions.
Finally, teacher roles emerged as a central contextual factor.
When teachers were perceived primarily as managers of learning processes, student agency was consistently lower.
In contrast, supervisory and partnership-oriented roles were associated with higher levels of agency, especially in participatory dimensions.
These findings resonate with prior research emphasizing facilitative and autonomy-supportive teaching (Reeve & Shin, 2020), and the role of teachers as partners in learning (Robertson, 2017).
text.formatted: These findings resonate with prior research emphasizing facilitative and autonomy-supportive teaching <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Reeve & Shin, 2020)</ref>, and the role of teachers as partners in learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Robertson, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The findings extend prior research by showing that pedagogical practices shape not only students' participation but also the conditions and orientations through which different forms of agency become possible.

In this sense, the study shifts the focus from asking whether students are agentic to understanding how teaching practices contribute to shaping the conditions under which agency can be and is enacted across higher education contexts.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings.
First, the crosssectional design precludes conclusions about causality and directionality.
Future research should incorporate longitudinal data to examine both short-and long-term effects of pedagogical practices on student agency.
Second, the data were collected from a single university, which limits generalizability across broader institutional and sociocultural contexts.

At the same time, the inclusion of multiple courses across different disciplinary settings provides substantial within-institutional variation, enabling analysis of how student agency is differentially structured across pedagogical contexts.
Extending the analysis to multiple institutions would further strengthen the generalizability of these findings.
Third, the number of clusters in the multilevel analysis (47 courses) was relatively small in relation to the complexity of the model.
Future studies using complex multilevel models would benefit from larger numbers of groups to strengthen parameter stability.

Taking together, these limitations indicate that while the findings provide robust evidence of associations and multilevel patterning, further research is needed to examine causal pathways and the conditions under which these relationships hold across contexts.

This study advances research on higher education by conceptualizing student agency as a multidimensional and multilevel phenomenon comprising three interrelated components: resources for agency, agentic will, and agentic action.
By integrating these components within a single framework, the study contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of how agency is structured, experienced, and enacted in higher education.
These findings demonstrate that student agency is not a fixed individual attribute but a context-sensitive and unevenly distributed phenomenon that varies both across individuals and between courses.
By examining variation across 47 courses spanning different disciplinary contexts, the study provides empirical evidence indicating that agency is systematically shaped by course-level conditions.
Importantly, the results show that teaching practices contribute to conditions under which student agency is enacted.
Transparent course design, cognitively demanding learning activities, and teacher roles which emphasize supervision and partnership were consistently linked to multiple dimensions of student agency.
These findings suggest that pedagogical arrangements shape opportunities available to students and can contribute to their agentic will and agentic action realized within learning environments.

Taken together, the findings of the study provide insights into the relationships among different components of student agency and propose a model for examining the dynamics of agency through the interplay between the agency resources afforded by pedagogical design, the students' agentic will, and the agentic action enacted within learning environments and student communities.

This underscores the need to design courses that integrate transparent structures, cognitively challenging tasks, and meaningful interaction in order to foster students' capacity for purposeful learning and transformation in higher education.

By providing a multidimensional, multilevel, empirically grounded framework, the study offers a basis for further research on how student agency is constituted, and how it varies across contexts, and can be supported through pedagogical practices.

To identify a refined theory-based model, consecutive exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analyses (CFA) were conducted to establish a theoretically concise, consistent, and interpretable model for students' agentic resources, agentic will, and agentic action (e.g., Hoyle, 2023).

text.text: Items were omitted or replaced in some scales to ensure that each final factor would have at least three items.
The AUR-RWA Scale initially included 80 items: 53 assessing agency resources, 14 assessing agentic will, and 13 assessing agentic action.
The items were selected based on three criteria.

The first concerned the item's statistical properties in the model-items were excluded if they did not load onto any factor, showed strong cross-loadings to several factors, or had high residual covariance with other items.
The second criterion was the use of modification indices in the analyses.

The third criterion was the application of a theoretically based interpretation to ensure that the items would form a conceptually coherent factor and that the factors would align with the theoretical framework.
All analyses were conducted using Mplus Version 8.11 (Muthén & Muthén, 1998 -2017).

text.text: The EFA/CFA factor model was estimated with two-level specifications (withinand between-group levels), and the equality of factor loadings was tested across levels.
Model parameters were calculated using the weighted least squares mean and variance adjusted (WLSMV) estimator with chi-square testing.
WLSMV was chosen because the items were ordinal, and some were skewed (e.g., responses were limited to three of five categories).
The large sample size (n = 1,140) and the minimum group size of 10 individuals supported this approach (see Park, 2023).

text.text: Based on modification indices, 14 residual covariances were added to the model at both the within-and between-group levels.

text.text: The confirmed AUS-W Subscale model encompassed three latent factors: Striving for understanding, Will to engage in interactive learning, and Will to engage in joint problem-solving.
The standardized factor loadings ranged from .60 to .87, indicating strong associations between the items and their respective factors.
The residual correlation between the items skmo2 and skko3 was 0.681, and between skmo2 and skko4, 0.253.
These correlations were estimated only at the within-group level because the variance of skmo2 was zero at the between-group level.
At the between-group level, the standardized factor loadings ranged from .54 to 1.0, reflecting variations in the residual variances.
Some residual variance estimates were small and negative, and therefore fixed to zero.
The ICCs for the AUS-A Subscale factors were .095 (Intentional goal-directed learning), .145 (Collaborating with and supporting others), and .242 (Active impactful participation).
All ICCs were statistically significant at the p = .05 level.
Active impactful participation correlated strongly with Intentional goal-directed learning and Collaborating with and supporting others at both the within-and between-group levels.
